title: Groupe de Galois motivique : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the second sheet of Grothendieck's letter to Mumford dated Algiers, 1 Nov 1965. The letter is very probably the one printed in Mumford's Selected Papers vol. II (2010), which includes his correspondence with Grothendieck.

Context from the previous page: Grothendieck withdraws a 'rash' conjecture he had told Mumford. In modern terms it said roughly that every polarized (variation of) Hodge structure is 'algebraic', i.e. motivic or of geometric origin. He notes that this contradicts the Tate conjecture. The Tate conjecture implies the following: if X is smooth, connected and simply connected over C, a polarized family of Hodge structures on X^an that is algebraic must be constant. This is the shape of what later became Deligne's theorem of the fixed part (Hodge II, 1971): a geometric VHS with trivial monodromy is constant. Grothendieck observes that one easily writes down non-constant families on homogeneous spaces of affine groups. These are the tautological families on flag domains, e.g. the compact duals Q-check of the next page. One hopes they are non-algebraic, as the Tate conjecture requires. With hindsight they fail Griffiths transversality (Griffiths 1968), which explains why they cannot be geometric.

This page then proposes a test case: a single polarized Hodge structure V 'with even partial degrees', i.e. h^{p,q} ≠ 0 only for p (hence q) even.
- Write the weight as w = p + q. Then p − q = w − 2q ≡ w (mod 4), so the Weil operator C = h(i) acts as a single scalar ±1.
- Hence the polarization form Q itself is (anti)definite.
- So the Hodge group G (the special Mumford–Tate group) has G_R compact; equivalently ad C, the Cartan involution, is trivial.
- The question: can such V be algebraic (motivic) unless G is commutative, i.e. V of CM type?
- Such structures are rigid. Griffiths transversality gives dF^p ⊂ F^{p-1} = F^p, so every VHS with these Hodge numbers is locally constant. The period domain (e.g. SO(2n)/U(n) in weight 2) is uncountable, while geometric ones are countable. So generic ones are certainly non-geometric, and the real question concerns special ones with non-commutative G.

Grothendieck makes it concrete for surfaces. Find Y smooth projective over C with H^{1,1} spanned by algebraic classes (ρ = h^{1,1}, 'maximal Picard number') and p_g = h^{0,2} ≥ 2. Then the transcendental lattice T(Y) is of type (2,0)+(0,2), giving exactly such a V.
- With p_g = 1 one knows examples (singular K3s, E×E with E CM), but there T has rank 2 and is CM.
- Note: as literally posed, the question already has an easy positive answer. Take products C×C' of curves whose Jacobians are isogenous to powers of one CM elliptic curve. Then H^1⊗H^1 is entirely algebraic in type (1,1), so ρ = h^{1,1} and p_g can be ≥ 2. But the transcendental part is then CM (commutative G), so this does not settle his real question.
- Within the Tannakian category generated by abelian varieties, the answer to the real question is 'only commutative'. A compact quotient of the Hodge group of an abelian variety must kill the semisimple part, since each Q-simple factor is non-compact at some real place where h is non-trivial.
- For general motives the question of a geometric Hodge structure with h^{p,q} concentrated in even p and non-commutative (compact) Mumford–Tate group is, to my knowledge, still not resolved.

The P.S. asks Mumford about his theta functions and whether he will write a book. That later became the Tata Lectures on Theta.
errors: As literally stated, the surface question (ρ = h^{1,1}, p_g ≥ 2) has easy positive answers, e.g. products of curves whose Jacobians are isogenous to E^g with E CM, or suitable Fermat-type surfaces. Grothendieck's parenthetical 'except when G is commutative' shows the intended question is about non-CM transcendental parts; the surface example as phrased does not isolate that.

The reduction 'even partial degrees ⇒ G_R compact' is correct: C = ±1 scalar makes the polarization definite. The parenthesis attaching the exception to 'can be algebraic' is an insertion, slightly ambiguous in placement but clear in meaning.

ideas.what: Tate conjecture implies an algebraic polarized family of Hodge structures over a simply connected base is constant; non-constant homogeneous families should therefore be non-algebraic
ideas.modern_name: Theorem of the fixed part / rigidity; non-horizontal families on flag domains violate Griffiths transversality
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Hodge II, 1971) for the fixed part; Griffiths (1968) for transversality
ideas.where_published: Letter likely in Mumford, Selected Papers II (2010), Grothendieck correspondence

ideas.what: Hodge structures with h^{p,q} supported on even p have compact Hodge group (Weil operator scalar, polarization definite)
ideas.modern_name: Compact Mumford–Tate / Hodge groups; Hodge structures of type (n,0,...,0,n) in even weight
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore following Mumford 1966 and Deligne; studied systematically later, e.g. Totaro (unsure of exact reference)
ideas.where_published: Same letter (Mumford Selected Papers II), if included

ideas.what: Question: can a geometric (motivic) Hodge structure with compact non-commutative Hodge group exist? Test case: surfaces with ρ = h^{1,1} and p_g ≥ 2
ideas.modern_name: Surfaces with maximal Picard number; CM-ness of rigid geometric Hodge structures
ideas.usually_credited_to: Beauville ('Some surfaces with maximal Picard number', 2014) for the surface examples; the MT-question is generally not attributed

missed.claim: Grothendieck poses the question whether a geometric Hodge structure with even Hodge types, hence compact Hodge group, must be CM (commutative Mumford–Tate group). For motives of abelian type it follows from the structure of Hodge groups of abelian varieties. In general it seems open and is rarely attributed to Grothendieck; the later literature on maximal-Picard-number surfaces and rigid Hodge structures usually does not cite this 1965 formulation.
missed.quote: I wonder if a single Hodge-structure V with even partial degrees (therefore giving rise to a "Hodge-group" G s.th. G_R is compact) can be algebraic (except when G is commutative)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A geometric counterexample, or a proof of CM-ness, would say something about motives outside the abelian-type category. It also connects to whether transcendental lattices of surfaces with ρ = h^{1,1} are always CM.

missed.claim: The Tate conjecture is used as the heuristic for constancy of algebraic families over simply connected bases, i.e. the theorem of the fixed part / Griffiths transversality obstruction, before either was available. This is an arithmetic route to a Hodge-theoretic rigidity statement.
missed.quote: if X is a smooth, connected simply connected scheme over C ... then V is "algebraic" only if it is a constant family
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is mainly of historical interest: it documents Grothendieck anticipating, via ℓ-adic heuristics, the non-geometricity of general period-domain families.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a known letter (likely published in Mumford's Selected Papers II). Its interest is the early, precise formulation of the compact-Hodge-group/CM question and the Tate-conjecture route to fixed-part rigidity, but the surface question as posed has easy answers and the ideas are largely part of later standard theory.
transcription_corrections: The insertion '(except when G is commutative)' is written above the end of the line containing 'Hodge-group' and belongs before the final '.' after 'can be algebraic'; the transcription places it correctly in substance.
'G s.th. G_R is compact' — in the image, 'compact' is underlined; 'cannot' and 'even partial degrees' are also underlined.
